specPoints.text: describe the structure of a transformer and understand that a transformer changes the size of an alternating voltage by having different numbers of turns on the input and output sides
explain the use of step-up and step-down transformers in the large-scale generation and transmission of electrical energy

primer.text: Two coils, one iron core, and an alternating input: the transformer rescales an alternating voltage by the turns ratio. This note builds the structure, sorts step-up from step-down, and follows the pair out onto the National Grid, where high voltage means cool cables.

lessons.title: Transformer structure and the alternating requirement
lessons.opening: A transformer is two coils sharing an iron core: the primary takes the input voltage, the secondary delivers the output, and the core carries the changing field between them. It rescales an alternating voltage — bigger or smaller by the turns ratio — and only alternating works, because a steady field through the secondary would induce nothing.
keyPoints: A transformer has a primary coil, a secondary coil and a shared iron core.
The primary coil is connected to the input alternating voltage.
The changing field in the core threads the secondary coil and induces its output.
A transformer rescales the size of an alternating voltage.
A steady direct input induces nothing in the secondary.

low.restatement: Two coils of wire wrapped on one iron ring. Feed alternating current into the first coil and a changed voltage appears across the second — bigger or smaller depending on the turns.
low.analogy: The core is a conveyor belt for changing fields: the primary places its alternating field on the belt, and the secondary unloads whatever comes round.
low.examPointer: Structure marks need all three parts named — primary coil, secondary coil, iron core — plus the alternating input stated.

medium.restatement: The primary's alternating current makes a continuously changing field in the core; that changing field threads the secondary turn by turn and induces its output voltage, whose size the turns ratio sets. A constant direct current gives a constant core field, so the secondary sees no change and induces nothing — the alternating requirement is the induction trigger, not a design preference.
medium.analogy: A transformer is a relay runner who only passes the baton while it is moving: a runner standing still (steady DC) never hands anything over.
medium.examPointer: If asked why DC fails, answer 'the field through the secondary is not changing, so nothing is induced' — naming the trigger earns the mark.

check.stem: Which parts make up the structure of a transformer?

options.text: primary coil, secondary coil and iron core
options.explanation: These three are the transformer's structure.

options.text: a single coil and a permanent magnet
options.explanation: Transformers need two coils and no permanent magnet.
Those belong to motors and dynamos.

options.text: a battery and a plastic core
options.explanation: Neither belongs in a transformer's structure.

check.stem: Which coil of a transformer is connected to the input supply?

options.explanation: Primary takes the input; secondary gives the output.
The secondary delivers the induced output.

options.text: both coils share the input equally
options.explanation: Input and output are separate windings.

options.text: neither — the core carries the input
options.explanation: The core carries the field, not the input connection.

check.stem: A transformer is supplied with steady direct voltage. The secondary output is:

options.text: zero, because the core field is not changing
options.explanation: Induction needs a changing field through the secondary.
No change, no induction, no output.
A steady input gives no output at all.
Turns ratio cannot rescue a non-changing field.

check.stem: What does a transformer change about its input?

options.text: the size of the alternating voltage
options.explanation: The turns ratio sets the output voltage size.
The output alternates at the same frequency as the input.
Transformers pass alternating output; rectifiers make DC.
Transformers transfer energy; they do not create it.

check.stem: Why must the input to a transformer be alternating?

options.text: the secondary only induces while the core field keeps changing
options.explanation: A changing field is the induction trigger.

options.text: direct current would melt the primary coil
options.explanation: Heating is not the reason transformers need AC.

options.text: the iron core only carries alternating fields
options.explanation: The core carries any field; only CHANGE induces.

options.text: the turns ratio only works for AC voltages
options.explanation: The ratio is geometry; the AC need is induction itself.

check.stem: State the three structural parts of a transformer.
check.modelAnswer: A primary coil, a secondary coil, and a shared iron core.

check.stem: State what kind of supply a transformer requires and why.
check.modelAnswer: An alternating supply, because the secondary only has a voltage induced while the core's field is changing.

check.stem: Explain how the input voltage's change reaches the secondary coil.
check.modelAnswer: The alternating current in the primary makes the core's magnetic field grow and shrink continuously. That changing field threads every turn of the secondary coil, and a changing field through a coil induces a voltage across it — so the primary's alternating behaviour is relayed to the secondary as an induced alternating output.

check.stem: A student connects a battery to a transformer's primary and a meter to its secondary. State the meter reading at switch-on, after it settles, and at switch-off — and explain the pattern.
check.modelAnswer: At switch-on the field through the core changes for a moment, so the meter kicks briefly; while the battery holds steady the field stops changing and the meter reads zero; at switch-off the field collapses, giving a brief kick the other way. Only CHANGES in the core field induce — steady DC gives steady zero.

lessons.title: Step-up and step-down transformers
lessons.opening: The turns ratio is the transformer's gear lever: more turns on the secondary than the primary steps the voltage up; fewer turns steps it down. Same changing field, same frequency — only the size of the alternating voltage changes, set entirely by the numbers of turns on the two sides.
keyPoints: A step-up transformer has more secondary turns than primary turns and raises the voltage.
A step-down transformer has fewer secondary turns than primary turns and lowers the voltage.
The output size is set by the ratio of turns wound on the two coils.
The output stays alternating at the same frequency as the input.
Equal turns on both sides give an output equal to the input voltage.

low.restatement: Count the turns: more on the output side means the voltage is stepped up; fewer means stepped down; equal means unchanged.
low.analogy: The turns ratio is a gearbox: a big output cog spins the voltage up, a small one winds it down, and equal cogs hold it level.
low.examPointer: Match the names to the turn counts explicitly — 'step-up: more secondary turns' — the pairing is the marked fact.

medium.restatement: Every secondary turn shares the same changing core field, so each turn contributes the same induced voltage increment; the secondary total is that increment times the secondary turn count, while the primary's input sets the per-turn value — hence the output scales with the turns ratio. The transformation alters magnitude only: frequency and alternating character pass through.
medium.analogy: Each secondary turn is one bucket under the same dripping field: ten turns fill ten buckets' worth, one turn fills one.
medium.examPointer: Comparing two transformers: read the turns FIRST, then name step-up or step-down — reversing the pairing loses the mark even with correct working.

check.stem: A transformer has more turns on the secondary than on the primary. It is a:

options.explanation: More secondary turns raise the output voltage.
Step-down needs fewer secondary turns.
Dynamos rotate; transformers are static.

options.text: transformer with equal input and output voltages
options.explanation: Equal voltages need equal turns.

check.stem: What happens to the output voltage when the primary has 200 turns and the secondary has 50?

options.text: it is stepped down to a quarter of the input
options.explanation: 50/200 is a quarter — fewer output turns, lower voltage.
That reads the ratio backwards.
Equal voltages need equal turns.
Fewer turns lower the voltage; they do not remove it.

check.stem: Which quantity passes through a transformer unchanged?

options.text: the frequency of the alternating voltage
options.explanation: The core field alternates at the input frequency.
Changing voltage size is the transformer's whole job.
The two coils have different turns by design.
Different windings have different resistances.

check.stem: A mains adapter must convert 230 V to a safe low voltage for a toy. Which transformer suits?

options.text: a step-down transformer with fewer secondary turns
options.explanation: Lowering the voltage needs fewer output turns.

options.text: a step-up transformer with more secondary turns
options.explanation: That would raise the already-high mains voltage.
Generators make electricity from motion; adapters transform it.

options.text: a transformer with equal turns on both coils
options.explanation: Equal turns leave the voltage unchanged at 230 V.

check.stem: The turns on a transformer's secondary are increased while the primary is untouched. The output voltage:

options.text: increases in proportion to the added turns
options.explanation: Output scales with the secondary turn count.
More secondary turns raise the output.
The output stays alternating regardless of turns.
Adding turns never cancels the output.

check.stem: State the turns relationship in a step-up transformer.
check.modelAnswer: A step-up transformer carries more turns on its secondary winding than on its primary.

check.stem: State what happens to the frequency of the voltage across a transformer.
check.modelAnswer: The frequency is unchanged: the output alternates at the same rate as the input.

check.stem: Explain why equal turns on both coils give an output equal to the input.
check.modelAnswer: The changing core field induces the same voltage per turn in both windings, because both share the identical field. With equal numbers of turns, the same per-turn voltage is summed the same number of times on each side, so the output matches the input voltage — the turns ratio of one passes the size through unchanged.

check.stem: Two transformers run from the same 12 V AC supply: one steps up to 48 V, the other steps down to 3 V. Compare their turns ratios and classify each.
check.modelAnswer: The 48 V unit has four times the primary turns on its secondary — a 4:1 secondary-to-primary ratio — so it is a step-up transformer. The 3 V unit has a quarter of the primary turns on its secondary — a 1:4 ratio — so it is a step-down transformer.

lessons.title: Transformers on the grid: transmission at high voltage
lessons.opening: The National Grid moves energy at very high voltage, and transformers are why: step-up transformers raise the voltage at the power station so the current falls, which slashes the energy lost as heat in the cables. Step-down transformers then lower the voltage safely for homes and factories.
keyPoints: Step-up transformers raise the voltage before electricity is transmitted across the grid.
At higher transmission voltage the cable current is lower for the same power.
A lower cable current wastes less energy as heat in the cables.
Step-down transformers lower the voltage for safe local use.
The transformer pair — step-up then step-down — brackets the long transmission lines.

low.restatement: Power stations step the voltage UP for the long journey, so less energy is wasted heating the cables; near your home it is stepped DOWN to a safe level.
low.analogy: It is like carrying water in a narrow pipe: pump at high pressure (voltage) so only a thin flow (current) is needed, and little is lost to friction on the way.
low.examPointer: Transmission answers need the chain: higher voltage → lower current → less heat loss. Quoting only 'high voltage' misses the reasoning.

medium.restatement: For a fixed transmitted power, raising the voltage proportionally lowers the current; cable heating scales with the square of the current, so the saving compounds at every voltage increase. Step-up transformers make the high-voltage transmission possible and step-down units restore safe levels at the consumer end — the 6.18P role split between the two transformer families.
medium.analogy: High-voltage transmission is carpooling for energy: pack the same passengers (power) into fewer vehicles (current) so the road (cable) heats up far less.
medium.examPointer: Use the word 'heat' or 'wasted energy' with 'lower current' — 'less resistance' is wrong: the cable is unchanged; only the current differs.

check.stem: Why is electricity transmitted across the grid at very high voltage?

options.text: the lower current then wastes less energy as heat in the cables
options.explanation: High voltage means low current for the same power.

options.text: high voltage makes the cables stronger
options.explanation: Voltage does not change cable mechanics.

options.text: high voltage is required by the transformers only
options.explanation: Transformers set the voltage; the REASON is the heat saving.

options.text: electricity travels faster at high voltage
options.explanation: Speed is not the reason; heating is.

check.stem: Which transformer sits at the power-station end of the grid?

options.explanation: The voltage is raised before the long journey.
Step-down units sit at the consumer end.
The generator makes the electricity; the transformer raises the voltage.

options.text: no transformer — the generator outputs the grid voltage
options.explanation: Step-up transformers bridge generator and grid.

check.stem: What do step-down transformers do near consumers?

options.text: lower the transmission voltage to safe levels
options.explanation: Step-down units make the supply usable and safe.

options.text: raise the voltage for the cables
options.explanation: That is the step-up role at the station.

options.text: convert AC to DC for homes
options.explanation: Homes receive AC; rectification is separate.
Transformers transfer; they do not store.

check.stem: For the same transmitted power, raising the transmission voltage tenfold makes the cable current:

options.explanation: Power = voltage × current, so current falls with rising voltage.
That inverts the power relationship.
Current and voltage trade off at fixed power.
Current falls but never to zero while power flows.

check.stem: Lower current in the transmission cables means:

options.text: less energy wasted heating the cables
options.explanation: Cable heating falls sharply as current falls.

options.text: more energy wasted in the cables
options.explanation: The loss falls with the current.
Current is what heats the cables.
The transmitted power is fixed; only the split changes.

check.stem: State which transformer type raises the voltage for transmission.
check.modelAnswer: A step-up transformer raises the voltage at the power-station end of the grid.

check.stem: State why a lower cable current is wanted on the grid.
check.modelAnswer: A lower current wastes less energy as heat in the transmission cables.

check.stem: Explain the full chain from step-up transformer to cooler cables.
check.modelAnswer: The step-up transformer raises the transmission voltage, so for the same transmitted power the current in the cables is lower. Cable heating is caused by the current, so the reduced current wastes less energy as heat — more of the generated power reaches the consumer end, where step-down transformers restore a safe voltage.

check.stem: A grid link loses noticeable energy as cable heat. The operators raise the transmission voltage using stronger step-up transformers. Describe and explain the change in the link's losses.
check.modelAnswer: The losses fall. With the transmitted power fixed, the higher voltage lets the same power flow at a lower current, and it is the current that heats the cables. The reduced current therefore wastes less energy as cable heat, so more of the generated energy arrives at the far end.

glossary.definition: A primary coil, secondary coil and iron core that change the size of an alternating voltage.
A transformer with more secondary than primary turns that raises the voltage.
A transformer with fewer secondary than primary turns that lowers the voltage.
